title: LinkedIn Premium – Is the paid version worth it?
excerpt: In today's professional digital landscape, LinkedIn is no longer just a virtual business card or a place to keep your CV online. It has become a key tool for building business relationships, for recruitment, and for picking up knowledge. For plenty of people on the free version, the basic features are enough for the occasional scroll through the newsfeed. But the moment your ambitions grow and your goals get more specific — whether in sales or in your career — the question of LinkedIn Premium comes up on its own.
metaTitle: LinkedIn Premium – Is the paid version worth it?
metaDescription: When your ambitions grow and your goals get more specific — whether in sales or in your career — the question of LinkedIn Premium comes up on its own.

runs.text: Is the paid version just a prestige badge next to your profile photo, or a serious accelerator for everything you do?

The decision to move to a LinkedIn Premium subscription shouldn't be made on impulse. It's an investment that has to pay for itself in the form of a new job, potential clients or skills you've picked up. Right now LinkedIn offers several account variants, matched to different industries and different user needs. Understanding the differences between them is critical if you don't want to burn budget on tools you'll never touch. In this article we'll take each option apart, look at what sits behind the paid options and tell you who the subscription will be a bullseye for.

Effective, professional LinkedIn management takes more than showing up regularly — it takes access to data the free version keeps hidden. Plenty of personal branding experts point out that a Premium account unlocks the analytics side of things, letting you understand who visits your profile and why. That knowledge is what lets you tune what you are doing, whether you're a freelancer chasing work or a manager angling for a promotion. A LinkedIn Premium account becomes a kind of command center, giving you an edge over users who stick to the basic features.
Subscription types – which plan should you pick?

The platform has split its offer into four main variants, each answering a different market need. The first, and the one individuals pick most often, is LinkedIn Premium Career (the Career account). It's built for people who are actively looking for work and want to stand out from the competition. The second option is LinkedIn Premium Business, aimed at people who want to grow their network and strengthen their company's position. After those come the heavy sales and recruitment tools: Sales Navigator Core and Recruiter Lite.

Which plan is right for you is tightly tied to what you actually do all day. If your bread and butter is running social media for clients, managing a company's image or B2B marketing in the broad sense, the Business version or Sales Navigator will hand you the insights you need. If, on the other hand, your goal is to change employers quickly, the sales tools are money you don't need to spend. Worth noting: LinkedIn allows for flexibility — you can test different plans, and the latest update to the interface makes managing a subscription more intuitive than ever.
LinkedIn Premium Career – a turbocharger for job seekers

Let's start with Premium Career. This Career account is designed to maximize your chances in the eyes of recruiters. One of the most important premium features in this variant is the option to be a Featured Applicant. That means your application shows up at the top of the recruiter's list, which drastically raises the odds that your professional experience gets noticed at all. On top of that, you get access to information about how you stack up against other candidates — you can see their level of education and their key skills, which lets you prepare better for the interview.

What's more, Premium Career gives you access to InMail messages. On the free version you can only write to people already in your network. With InMail credits you can message a recruiter or a headhunter directly, even if you aren't connected. That's a powerful tool for going after a job proactively. Users on this plan also get full access to the LinkedIn Learning education platform, which makes it quick to fill in the new skills job ads are asking for.
LinkedIn Premium Business – for growing your network and your company

For entrepreneurs and business owners who aren't necessarily looking for a job but do want to grow the business, there's the LinkedIn Premium Business plan. It combines the qualities of the Career account with analytics tools. The key value here is unlimited profile browsing (on the free version that limit runs out fast once you're researching seriously) plus wider access to company statistics (Business Insights). That lets you analyze hiring trends at competitors or at business partners, which is priceless market knowledge.

On the Business plan you also get more InMail message credits than on Career (usually 15 a month). It's ideal for opening business relationships with decision makers outside your network. Keep in mind that deliberate personal brand building rests on reaching the right audience, and Premium Business removes the communication barriers, letting you take an offer of collaboration or a partnership proposal straight to the CEOs and directors who would otherwise be out of your reach.
Sales Navigator – the weapon of mass destruction in B2B sales

If your goal is aggressively building a lead list and selling, the standard plans may turn out not to be enough. This is where LinkedIn Sales Navigator comes in. It isn't simply a paid version of the platform — it's close to a separate ecosystem built for social selling. Sales Navigator offers advanced search filters that aren't available on any other plan. You can filter potential clients not only by job title or industry, but by company size, revenue, and even by whether a given user has published anything in the last 30 days.

In the Sales Navigator version, the algorithms suggest contacts who might be interested in your services on their own, learning from the choices you've made before. You can build dedicated account and lead lists, watch for personnel changes at companies you care about, and get a notification when a prospect gets promoted or changes jobs. For sales departments this tool is an absolute standard. Sales Navigator saves hundreds of hours of manual research, delivering “warm” contacts almost on a plate.
Recruiter Lite – support for HR

The last of the main pillars is Recruiter Lite. It's a tool built for headhunters and small recruitment agencies. It allows advanced candidate search, managing recruitment projects and tracking the history of contact with a given person. Unlike Sales Navigator, which is focused on selling, Recruiter Lite is optimized for finding talent. It lets recruiters see full candidate profiles (even people beyond the 3rd degree of connection) and use 30 InMail messages a month to invite them into recruitment processes.
The “Who viewed your profile” feature – why does it matter so much?

Whichever plan you choose, one of the most sought-after features is the full list of people who have visited your profile. On the free version you see only the last few, and the rest are blurred out. On the Premium version (any of them) you get the full list from the last 90 days (or 365 days, depending on the variant). Why does that matter? Because someone looking at your profile is already showing a degree of interest. It's the perfect pretext for getting in touch (“Hi, I saw you stopped by my profile…”).

For salespeople it can be a signal that a client is weighing up the offer. For job seekers, a sign that a recruiter is looking at their application. Tracking those visits lets you judge how effective they are and check whether what you're doing (publishing posts, for instance) is pulling in the right target audience. If you're aiming at marketing directors and your profile is mostly visited by students, that's a sign you need to change your communication strategy or the keywords in your headline.
LinkedIn Learning – education included in the subscription

One service deserves its own paragraph, because it is routinely underrated and it is an enormous piece of added value across every Premium plan — LinkedIn Learning. It's a library of thousands of professional video courses run by experts from all over the world. The subjects range from programming through team management to using Excel or Photoshop. Importantly, when you finish a course you get a certificate you can add to your profile with a single click, in the “Licenses and certifications” section.

Access to the LinkedIn Learning education platform saves you on the order of several hundred zloty a month, if you compare it with course prices on other e-learning platforms. For an employer, the sight of a candidate who keeps upgrading their qualifications through this platform is a signal that they're proactive. Inside your own company you can use these resources to train staff, if you go for the team packages. It's an excellent way to make progress on your professional goals without leaving the house.
Is it worth investing? A cost and benefit analysis

So, to the key question: is LinkedIn Premium worth it? The answer depends on how intensively you use the service. The subscription isn't cheap — prices start at around 100 zloty a month for the Career plan and climb into the hundreds for Sales Navigator (prices can vary depending on whether you're billed monthly or annually, and on the promotions running at the time). If you log into LinkedIn once a week to scroll the feed, the paid version will be money spent for nothing.

That said, if LinkedIn is a work tool for you — you're looking for clients, recruiting, or desperately need a new job — it's worth the investment. The cost of a monthly subscription is negligible next to the commission on a single B2B client won, or the raise that comes with a new job. Treat it as a business tool. It's also worth noting that paying annually gets you a significant discount, which makes the premium plans more affordable.
How do you test Premium safely?

The platform is confident about the value of its services, which is why LinkedIn usually offers a free month of trial to new users (or to people who haven't had Premium in a long time). It's the best way to find out first-hand what the advanced features are good for. To activate the trial you'll have to give payment details, but remember that you can cancel the subscription at any moment before the trial period ends, at no cost at all.

During that month, use every tool you can get at: run through a dozen or so courses on LinkedIn Learning, spend the InMail credits and lean hard on prospect search. Only after a “crash test” like that will you be able to judge whether these features really translate into your results. Remember too that after you cancel the subscription you keep access to your profile and your network — you only lose the exclusive features and the history of your analytics data.

To sum up, a LinkedIn Premium account is a powerful ace up your sleeve in the professional world. Whether you pick Premium Career, Premium Business or Sales Navigator, you gain a technological and informational edge. In an age of digital transformation, knowing who is watching you and being able to reach decision makers directly often decides professional success.
FAQ – frequently asked questions
Can a LinkedIn Premium subscription be written off as a business expense?

Yes — if the premium account is used for business purposes such as finding potential clients, marketing or recruitment, the invoice for the subscription can usually be booked as a tax-deductible cost in your company. LinkedIn issues invoices, which you can download in the payment settings.
What happens to my data after I cancel a Premium subscription?

Once you cancel the Premium version, your account goes back to the free version. You lose access to the advanced features, such as the full list of profile visitors, the advanced search filters and LinkedIn Learning. Your profile, your network of professional contacts and your messages, however, stay untouched.
Does Sales Navigator include the Premium Business features?

Yes — Sales Navigator is a higher plan than Premium Business. Beyond the dedicated sales interface, it offers most of the features available on the Business plan, such as access to LinkedIn Learning, extended insight into who viewed your profile, and a larger number of InMail messages (usually 50 a month), which makes it a comprehensive tool for salespeople.
